title: AI Product Placement Disclosure Rules: FTC, ASA, Ofcom, the EU, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram
summary: A product added in post-production is still a paid placement. What the FTC, the UK's ASA and Ofcom, the EU's Audiovisual Media Services Directive and the YouTube, TikTok and Instagram settings ask of it, and how to label a virtual placement and every clip cut from it.
body_markdown:
A paid product placement has to be disclosed whether a props team put it on the table or software added it afterwards. The rules are about the commercial relationship, not about how the product got into the picture. In the US, the FTC expects a clear disclosure in the video itself. In the UK, the ASA expects online ads to be obviously identifiable, and Ofcom requires a neutral logo on placements in programmes a broadcaster made or commissioned. In the EU, the Audiovisual Media Services Directive requires viewers to be told at the start and end of a programme and after each ad break. YouTube, TikTok and Instagram each have a paid-content setting that the creator is expected to turn on.


If you produce placements with[Overlap Product Lab](https://overlap.ai/product-lab) , the same rules apply to them as to a product that was on set. Product Lab adds only the product and its shadow and leaves the people and the set as they were filmed, so the main question a placement raises is the advertising one: was it paid for, and is it labelled.


This is a practical summary, not legal advice, and the rules change. The sources are linked where they are cited and were checked on October 27, 2026; confirm the current wording in your market before relying on it. Where a placement is commercially significant, have someone qualified in the market you publish to review the disclosure.


## Does a virtual placement need the same disclosure as a real one?


Yes. None of the rules below turns on production method. The FTC asks about the financial relationship between a creator and a brand. The ASA asks whether a viewer can tell that content is an ad. The EU directive treats product placement as including a product in a programme in return for payment. A product rendered into a scene in post-production meets each of those descriptions exactly as a real one would.


What is different about a virtual placement is practical. It is often added to an episode where nobody mentions the product, so there is no host read to carry the disclosure, and it travels into every short clip cut from the placed shots. Both affect how it should be labelled, and the checklist further down covers both.


## What does the FTC require in the United States?


The FTC's guidance for creators,[Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers) , says to disclose any "financial, employment, personal, or family relationship" with a brand, including free or discounted products. For video, it is specific:


- "The disclosure should be in the video and not just in the description." Disclosing in both the audio and the video is better.
- In a livestream, repeat the disclosure periodically so that people who join late see it.
- Use plain words such as "ad" or "sponsored", and avoid abbreviations such as "sp", "spon" and "collab".
- Use a platform's disclosure tool "in addition to your own, good disclosure", not instead of it.


The FTC's own FAQ adds that a platform's feature is "no guarantee that it's an effective way" to disclose, and that responsibility "rests with the influencer and the brand – not the platform".[FTC's Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/ftcs-endorsement-guides-what-people-are-asking)


The FTC's guidance is written around endorsements, and a silent product on a creator's table is an implied one: viewers reasonably take a product on a show's set as something the show is associated with. If a brand paid for its product to be seen in your video, treat the video as sponsored and disclose it in the video.


## What do the ASA and Ofcom require in the UK?


Two regulators cover two kinds of video.


**Online, the ASA.** The ASA's guidance on[recognising ads in social media and influencer marketing](https://www.asa.org.uk/advice-online/recognising-ads-social-media.html) , updated August 6, 2026, says labels such as "Ad", "Advert", "Advertising" and "Ad Feature" are very likely to be acceptable, with or without a hashtag, while "Sponsored", "Gifted" and "In association with" are unlikely to be clear enough. On YouTube, the ad label needs to be in the title or the thumbnail, so that viewers see it before they click. Instagram's "Paid partnership" label may be sufficient if it is upfront, clear and prominent, but the ASA notes that its 2026 research found the label may not be enough on its own.


**On broadcast television, Ofcom.**[Section Nine of the Ofcom Broadcasting Code](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/tv-radio-and-on-demand/broadcast-standards/section-nine-commercial-references-tv) governs product placement on UK TV. Placement in programmes produced or commissioned by the broadcaster, or a connected person, must be signalled with a universal neutral logo at the start of the programme, when it recommences after commercial breaks, and at the end. Placement in acquired programmes has no signalling requirement. The code also bars placement in certain genres, including news, children's, religious, consumer advice and current affairs programmes, and requires that placed products are not promoted or given undue prominence.


## What does the EU require?


Product placement in the EU is governed by Article 11 of the[Audiovisual Media Services Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2018/1808/oj) , as revised in 2018, which each member state implements in its own law. Under it:


- placement is allowed in audiovisual media services, except in news and current affairs, consumer affairs, religious and children's programmes;
- it must not affect editorial independence, directly encourage purchases or give the product undue prominence;
- viewers must be clearly informed of it at the start and the end of the programme, and when the programme resumes after an advertising break;
- placement of tobacco and e-cigarettes, and of prescription-only medicines and treatments, is banned outright.


National rules add detail on top, so check the implementing law in the country you publish to.


## What do YouTube, TikTok and Instagram ask creators to do?


Each platform has a setting for paid content, and each puts compliance with the law back on the creator.


Platform The setting What it does


**YouTube** In the upload details, select "Yes, my video includes branded content" Adds a disclosure label at the beginning of the video


**TikTok** "You must enable the commercial content disclosure toggle" Labels the post as paid or commercial content


**Instagram** Use the branded content tool to tag the brand partner, every time you post branded content Adds the "Paid partnership" label


Sources:[YouTube Help](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/154235) , the[TikTok Branded Content Policy](https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/global/bc-policy/en) , effective August 31, 2026, and[Instagram Help](https://help.instagram.com/1695974997209192) .


YouTube's page says creators and brands are "responsible for understanding and complying with all applicable legal requirements", and TikTok's policy says the same of "all applicable laws and regulations". In other words, the setting is the minimum, and it does not replace the disclosure in the video that the FTC and the ASA describe.


## Does a virtual placement need an AI or altered-content label?


That is a separate question from the advertising one. YouTube asks creators to disclose realistic content that has been altered or synthetically generated, and its examples centre on realistic representations of people and events that did not happen, such as replaced faces or generated voices. It does not require disclosure for clearly unrealistic content or for minor, primarily aesthetic edits.[YouTube Help](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/14328491)


A product composited onto a real table is not among YouTube's examples either way, so whether to mark it as altered content is a judgement. Two things help. A placement that leaves the people exactly as filmed is far from the face and voice cases the rule describes, whereas a generative edit that re-synthesises the hosts is much closer to them. And when a viewer could be misled about something that matters, disclosing is the safer choice.[Why generative video models change the rest of the shot](https://overlap.ai/blogs/why-generative-video-models-cant-do-product-placement) explains the difference between the two kinds of edit.


## A disclosure checklist for a virtual product placement


Where What to do


In the video An on-screen label at the start, such as "Ad" or "Includes paid product placement", or a spoken mention. For a long episode, repeat it after breaks


Platform setting YouTube's branded-content option, TikTok's commercial content toggle, Instagram's branded content tool


Title or thumbnail "Ad" before the click, where the ASA's YouTube guidance applies


Description Name the sponsor and say the product appears as a paid placement


Every clip A clip cut from a placed episode carries the product, so it is a new post that needs its own label and setting


Broadcast The neutral placement logo at the start, after breaks and at the end, where Ofcom or EU rules apply


Categories Check restrictions before placing tobacco, e-cigarettes, medicines, alcohol, gambling or food high in fat, salt or sugar


Records Keep the agreement and a list of every episode and clip that carries the placement


The clip row is the one most often missed. A placement in the wide shot of a podcast travels into every clip cut from that shot, and each of those clips is a separate post on a separate platform, often published days later. Label them when they are cut, not when someone notices.[Product placement for video podcasts](https://overlap.ai/blogs/podcast-product-placement) covers the rest of that workflow, and[How to do AI product placement](https://overlap.ai/blogs/how-to-do-ai-product-placement) puts the disclosure step into the production sequence.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Does AI product placement need to be disclosed?


Yes, when it is paid for. A product added to footage in post-production is advertising in the same way as one placed on set, so the sponsored-content rules of the country and platform where the video is published apply, including an in-video disclosure and the platform's paid-content setting.


### Is disclosure different for a virtual product placement than a real one?


The rules are the same, because they depend on the commercial relationship rather than on how the product got into the picture. In practice, a virtual placement often has no host read to carry the disclosure, so it usually needs an on-screen label or a spoken mention added to the video.


### Is YouTube's branded content setting enough to disclose a placement?


Usually not on its own. The FTC says a platform's tool should be used in addition to your own clear disclosure in the video, and the ASA expects an ad label in the title or thumbnail of a YouTube video before the viewer clicks.


### Do clips cut from an episode with a product placement need their own disclosure?


Yes. A clip cut from a placed shot carries the product, and it is published as a separate post, so it needs its own in-video label and its own paid-content setting on the platform where it is posted.


### What does Ofcom require for product placement on UK television?


For programmes produced or commissioned by the broadcaster or a connected person, Ofcom's Broadcasting Code requires product placement to be signalled with a universal neutral logo at the start, after commercial breaks and at the end. Acquired programmes have no signalling requirement, and placement is barred in genres such as news and children's programmes.


### What does EU law require for product placement?


Article 11 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive allows product placement except in news and current affairs, consumer affairs, religious and children's programmes. Viewers must be clearly informed at the start and end of the programme and after ad breaks, and placement of tobacco, e-cigarettes and prescription-only medicines is banned.
